Learn to read sheet music: eight-week practice guide

Build reading accuracy before increasing speed. This guide pairs musical concepts with the free interactive exercises in Notation Lab. Open a week to see its five practice steps.

Open the practice app. The guide remains readable without JavaScript.

Week 1: The musical alphabet

1. Map pitch to the staff

Read from the bottom line upward. Treble lines are E–G–B–D–F; bass lines are G–B–D–F–A. Spaces continue the same seven-letter sequence. Middle C is the shared landmark between the clefs. Identify the clef before naming any note.

2. Practise natural notes

In Note Trainer select Treble and Staff notes. Name each note before playing it. Work in short groups without revealing the answer. Repeat in Bass. Move between line and space notes rather than memorising only an acronym.

3. Read by interval

In Sight-Reading use Foundation. A neighbouring line-to-space movement is a step; line-to-next-line is a skip. Read the direction and distance before looking for an individual key.

4. Write and review

Start a Foundation writing exercise. Match the shown pitches and durations using the keyboard and note-length selector. Read your finished phrase aloud, then compare playback with the notation.

5. Checkpoint

Complete several accurate foundation sessions on different days. The Beginner part of each task bar grows from correct attempts with enough repetition; opening a lesson does not award mastery.

Week 2: Rhythm and timing

1. Understand note values

A semibreve lasts four crotchets, a minim two, a crotchet one, a quaver one half and a semiquaver one quarter. A dot adds half the original duration. Count values relative to the written metre rather than treating every denominator as a crotchet.

2. Count simple metre

Set Rhythm Lab to 2/4, 3/4 and 4/4 in turn. Begin at 60–80 crotchets per minute. Count denominator units aloud, then add “and” subdivisions. Tap the displayed rhythm, including every written onset.

3. Distinguish beat from subdivision

Switch between the quarter, eighth and mixed patterns. Keep the underlying pulse steady while placing extra onsets between it. In 2/2, a minim is the notated beat, while this app still sets tempo in crotchets per minute.

4. Write durations

Use the Composer duration selector to enter a bar with minims, crotchets and quavers. Add the values yourself and check the barline. Select and edit any incorrect value.

5. Checkpoint

Finish the daily rhythm requirement through active tapping. Practise multiple simple metres with consistent timing before raising tempo.

Week 3: Keys and accidentals

1. Learn accidental rules

A sharp raises a pitch by one semitone, a flat lowers it by one, and a natural cancels an accidental. In conventional notation an accidental applies to its staff position through the bar. A key signature establishes recurring alterations.

2. Build major scales

Use the interval pattern tone–tone–semitone–tone–tone–tone–semitone. Write C major, G major and F major on paper. Preserve one of each letter name in a scale; enharmonic spellings are not interchangeable for analysis.

3. Extend the range

In Note Trainer select With ledger lines. Locate middle C first, then count successive staff positions. Keep the clef in view. Use Z and X to reach the required register.

4. Read chromatic notation

Select Chromatic notes. Identify the letter and octave before applying the accidental. This app spells chromatic pitches with sharps; practise flat spellings separately on paper.

5. Checkpoint

Alternate clefs and difficulty rather than practising a single familiar range. Intermediate mastery requires successful intermediate attempts.

Week 4: Intervals and chords

1. Name intervals on the staff

Count both the starting and ending letter names for interval number. Then count semitones to determine quality: major, minor, perfect, augmented or diminished. A third spans three letter names even when chromatic.

2. Hear intervals

In Ear Training begin with single pitches and the reference C. Move to Intermediate two-note intervals. Sing the second note before playing it. Use Advanced to require the written register as well as pitch class.

3. Construct triads

On paper build major, minor, diminished and augmented triads from stacked thirds. Spell the root, third and fifth correctly. Identify root position, first inversion and second inversion from the bass note.

4. Connect reading and sound

Write a broken triad as a monophonic Composer phrase. Play it slowly and compare the heard contour with the staff. Simultaneous chord entry is outside this composer.

5. Checkpoint

Use interval challenges without the reveal button. Revealed or assisted answers do not earn mastery evidence.

Week 5: Two-clef reading

1. Use shared landmarks

Find treble G, bass F and middle C. Read outward by steps and skips. Keep the same sounding pitch when translating a note from treble to bass notation.

2. Alternate clefs

Set Note Trainer to Mixed and use ledger lines. Pause long enough to identify the clef, then reduce that pause over repeated sessions. Avoid guessing by the note’s screen height alone.

3. Read longer phrases

In Sight-Reading choose longer melodies. Use Intermediate for ledger-line reading and Advanced for chromatic pitches with exact octave matching. Scan the whole phrase before the first note.

4. Practise hands separately

Play treble phrases with the right hand and bass phrases with the left. For true two-staff, two-hand reading, use an external grand-staff score; this app displays one clef at a time.

5. Checkpoint

Finish unfamiliar melodies in both clefs. A restarted melody preserves previous errors in the background; it does not erase evidence.

Week 6: Writing real music

1. Plan a phrase

Choose a metre, a tonal centre and a four-bar contour. Decide where the phrase rests and resolves before entering pitches. Count the duration of every bar.

2. Apply engraving rules

Group beams according to the beat structure. Distinguish a tie, which extends the same pitch, from a slur, which groups different pitches. Dots change duration; stems and flags show the underlying note value.

3. Complete writing exercises

Move from Foundation to Intermediate dotted rhythms and Advanced chromatic phrases. Read the target notation and select the correct duration before each entry. Free composition counts as practice, but note quantity alone does not establish correctness.

4. Edit the full score

Select any note in the score or numbered list. Change pitch and length, apply the edit, and inspect the resulting bar divisions. Review early bars as well as the most recent notes.

5. Checkpoint

Export MIDI and inspect the phrase in Logic’s Score Editor. The app does not assess musical taste, harmony or expressive phrasing; its writing mastery assesses the displayed copying exercises.

Week 7: Advanced rhythm

1. Feel compound metre

Set 6/8, 9/8 and 12/8. Count in groups of three quavers: 1-la-li, 2-la-li. Distinguish two dotted-crotchet beats in 6/8 from three crotchet beats in 3/4.

2. Control additive grouping

Compare 2+3/8 with 3+2/8, then 2+2+3/8 with 3+2+2/8. Keep every eighth-note unit equal while moving the accents. Enter explicit groups rather than relying on the odd-metre default.

3. Read changing metres

Enter 4/4, 7/8, 6/8. Count through each transition without pausing or adding an extra unit. The entered sequence repeats. Keep the app’s crotchet-based tempo definition in mind.

4. Read smaller values

Use 5/16 or 7/16 slowly. Separate beat grouping from note duration. Study syncopation and tuplets from an external score; arbitrary tuplet entry is not implemented in this app.

5. Checkpoint

Advanced rhythm evidence requires accurate taps in changing/additive or fine-unit metre at a controlled tempo. Avoid increasing speed until the grouping remains stable.

Week 8: Musicianship

1. Scan before performing

Identify clef, metre, pitch range, repeated shapes, accidentals and difficult rhythmic positions before playing. Count one silent preparatory bar. Keep going after a recoverable mistake.

2. Transcribe a phrase

Listen to a short phrase, sing it, tap its rhythm, then write it. Use an external recording or a musical partner so the answer is not already visible. Check pitch and duration separately.

3. Compose and revise

Write a short original melody. Review notation, phrase shape, range and rhythmic clarity. Export to Logic for articulation, dynamics, slurs, harmony and a full score layout.

4. Maintain a balanced routine

Complete the five daily tasks through actual input. Return to weak task bars instead of repeatedly practising only the strongest skill. Export a progress backup periodically.

5. Final checkpoint

Master is the end of this app’s measured exercise scale. Reaching it requires sustained success across all three difficulty tiers. It is not certification of professional sight-reading, ensemble skill or complete musicianship.
